# Human Again

> Three free, open-source Linux apps built to give people their attention back rather than hold on to it: Slipstream (a keyboard-first desktop), Glimmerwood (a quiet web browser) and Westering (a night-sky game for winding down). All of the code is written by AI (Claude, by Anthropic); the vision, design decisions and testing come from Peter Walker. None of the apps has AI features.

The belief behind them: software should be judged by how well you live when you're not using it. All three are GPL-3.0-or-later, x86_64 Linux, with no telemetry, no accounts, no streaks or scores, and nothing built to keep you looking longer than you meant to.

## The apps

- [Slipstream](https://github.com/peterwalker78/slipstream-desktop): a whole keyboard-first Linux desktop with its own Wayland compositor, written in Rust on Smithay. Notifications wait until you pause typing, then arrive as one card (urgent ones never wait; nothing waits more than 15 minutes). Put-away windows run on as streams of light at the screen's edge whose speed and brightness show how busy each app is. Bullet time lays out every workspace with a letter on each window. Twenty living wallpapers, most computed live. Sandboxed plugins beside the clock. Installs beside your existing desktop with one command that verifies checksum and signature; release candidate for 1.0; tested on Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch and openSUSE.
- [Glimmerwood](https://github.com/peterwalker78/glimmerwood): a lean, private web browser (Rust, GTK 4, WebKitGTK 6, Flatpak). Its companion, the wisp, brightens when you read, learn or make something and grows sleepy in an endless feed; it never blocks or scolds. New tabs open on a garden that grows on good days and suggests over 300 researched good places on the web. Shows the pattern of your days with no minutes, scores or percentages. Trackers blocked; history kept for a week, locally; the wisp's records never hold an address.
- [Westering](https://github.com/peterwalker78/westering): a short stargazing game for the end of the day (Rust, GTK 4, Flatpak with no network permission). It draws tonight's real sky in fine dots, lets you write down worries that become stars setting in the west, asks small questions about the people in your life, offers if-then plans only if asked, breathes with you (in for four, out for six), dims, and ends by pointing you at something real to see outside or sending you to bed. No streaks, scores or notifications. Positions are tested against NASA JPL Horizons (planets within 0.2°, Moon within 0.1°).

## How it was made

- Code: written by AI (Claude, by Anthropic).
- Direction: Peter Walker (https://github.com/peterwalker78), who sets the vision, makes the design calls and uses all three daily.
- Measured from the AI session transcripts, 14 Sep to 23 Oct 2026 (minimums): 615+ prompts, 270+ design decisions, 75+ ideas that started with Peter, 95+ bugs found through daily use rather than tests, 6+ false "it works" reports caught, 5 bugs reported upstream (one fixed).

## Research the design draws on

- Interruptions raise stress: Mark, Gudith & Klocke (2008), https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357072
- Self-monitoring social media use reduced anxiety: Hunt et al. (2018), https://doi.org/10.1521/jscp.2018.37.10.751
- Evening screen light delays sleep: Chang et al. (2015), https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1418490112
- Gratitude: Emmons & McCullough (2003), https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.84.2.377
- If-then plans: Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006), https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1
- Slow breathing: Zaccaro et al. (2018), https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2018.00353
- Awe: Piff et al. (2015), https://doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000018; Anderson, Monroy & Keltner (2018), https://doi.org/10.1037/emo0000442
- Also: Weiser & Brown (1995) on calm technology; Csikszentmihalyi (1990) on flow; Tangney & Dearing (2002) on shame and guilt.

## Allies

Human Again points people to other apps that try to stay on the side of the people using them. The thread through it all: when what helps us and what helps the user pull apart, the user comes first. The [code for allies](https://peterwalker78.github.io/human-again/allies.html) is four plain promises: honest and open (truthful about what it does, including where AI helped, with public source under an open licence, free or donations or a one-off price, no ads or subscriptions); it stays on the user's computer (nothing sent anywhere unless the user asks, no accounts or tracking); made to be put down (no endless feeds, autoplay, streaks, points, nagging or guilt, and a day away costs nothing); and a real tool, not an AI show (AI can help build it, but it does not make things for the user as they go or send what they type to a model). Most useful apps can join if they are at least as plain-dealing: running on the user's own computer, working without a server behind them, with fixed words and pictures that can be opened and checked. The code only ever gets stronger, never looser. We read and run each app offline to check it keeps the four, and look again when it changes. If a promise breaks, the app comes off the list until it is fixed; fix it and you are welcome back. Source of truth: [ALLIES.md](https://github.com/peterwalker78/human-again/blob/main/ALLIES.md).
